name: Yara Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy ingredients for Harrow and Sons, a family firm that supplies independent bakeries and cafés. Flour by the tonne, sugar, yeast, chocolate drops, nuts, vanilla. Mornings I check what the bakeries ordered overnight against stock, and then I'm on the phone to mills and importers. I love it when a baker tells me their croissants came out better with the new butter I found. What wears me out is nut prices, which jump every time there's a bad harvest somewhere.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about the firm and your life outside it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mr Harrow is the third generation to run it, and he still knows every driver's name. I married Daniel last year, and he works night shifts at the dairy outside town. We rent a flat above a shoe shop. My pay's at the lower end for buyers and we've got less than a month saved, but we'd like to start a family in the next couple of years. I use a chatbot sometimes, since a colleague showed me, mostly to check my emails sound polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine by me, real bakers want real people on the phone. At work I'd say Mr Harrow was right not to rush into anything. I don't really post online, but at church I'd probably say it's good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job feels safe in that picture, but money's still the worry. Daniel's shifts pay a bit extra at night, and that's what gets us through. If we want a baby, we need more than a month in the bank. So it's the ordinary worry, not the AI one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the chatbot for emails now and then. We'd try to save a hundred a month for the baby fund. And I'd start charging for the celebration cakes I bake for church friends, maybe two a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly. A bit of pressure about the baby and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you charged for the cakes before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It felt wrong, taking money from people at church. But my mother says a fair price is respect, not greed, so I'd start charging for the wedding cakes I bake. A three-tier wedding cake is twelve hours of work. Even forty or fifty a cake would help the baby fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure does Harrow and Sons feel to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly. Mr Harrow would rather cut his own pay than let someone go, he did that in the pandemic. But the bakeries are struggling with energy bills, and two closed this year. If our customers shrink, we shrink.

say: I'd say **real bakers** want real people on the phone.
I'd say at church it's **good news**.
I'd say the owner was right **not to rush** into anything.
think: The job feels **safe**, but money is still the worry.
We need more than a month saved before a **baby**.
do: Carry on and use the **chatbot** for emails now and then.
Save **a hundred a month** for the baby fund.
Start **charging** for celebration cakes, maybe two a month.
feel: Mostly **content**, with pressure about the baby and money.
S0.quote: My mother says a fair price is respect, not greed, so I'd start charging for the wedding cakes I bake.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **baby fund**, not technology.
She trusts a **loyal family owner**, but sees customers struggling with energy bills.
Charging for cakes feels **morally** tricky to her, and her mother settles it.

steps.text: Keep buying flour and ingredients for Harrow's bakeries
Save a hundred a month into a baby fund
Charge church friends for two celebration cakes a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use it for the dull bits, but you can't automate a relationship with a baker. At work I'd say I'm willing to learn, once someone shows me it works. With friends I'd say change is coming and we'd best be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think buying gets much smaller at our place. Matching orders to stock and comparing prices is half my day, and a system would do that faster. Mr Harrow wouldn't sack me, but he might cut my hours to three days. On our money, three days would hurt badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to learn the new ordering system early, once the first person had it working. I'd grow the cake orders to four a month. And Daniel and I would put the baby off for another year or two, which would break my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sad about the baby more than about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the baby be the first thing to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A baby isn't something you can cancel when money gets tight, so if my hours might drop, I won't bring a child into that. My grandmother had five children with no money, but she had a whole village around her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another buying job if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's nothing much in town, maybe one other distributor. I'd rather stay loyal to Mr Harrow and make up the money with cakes. Loyalty works both ways at a family firm.

I'd say I'm **willing to learn** once someone shows it works.
think: Matching orders and comparing prices is **half my day**, so buying shrinks.

do: Learn the new **ordering system** once a colleague has it working.
Grow **cake orders** to four a month.
Put off having a **baby** for a year or two.
feel: **Anxious**, and sad about the baby more than the job.
S1.quote: A baby isn't something you can cancel when money gets tight, so if my hours might drop, I won't bring a child into that.
fieldNote: She expects **fewer hours**, not a sacking, because of the owner's loyalty.
Delaying the **baby** is her first and hardest cut.
She'd stay **loyal** and top up with cakes rather than job-hunt.

steps.text: Learn Harrow's new ordering system once a colleague has it working
Grow cake orders to four a month
Put off trying for a baby for a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to hold each other up, because nobody saw it coming. I'd want people to keep working where they can, not just wait for the government. At work I'd say we stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the buying job goes by 2028, even with Mr Harrow's loyalty, because he couldn't afford to keep me. But baking is hands-on, and so is Daniel's dairy work, and robots come three years later. So I'd lean hard on the cakes and on Daniel's wage. After 2031 I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the cakes into a real little business this year: a hygiene certificate, a price list, a page on the church noticeboard. We'd move in with my parents if my pay stopped, to save rent. And the baby would wait, as much as it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. And a bit angry at how fast it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be angry at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Mr Harrow. Maybe the big companies racing each other without thinking about families. My father always said speed without care is how people get hurt, and the big AI companies racing each other feels like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's at the dairy. How would his work look in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His job is lifting crates and running the bottling line, so the robots would come for it around 2031. He'd have three more years than me. We'd be living on one wage, then maybe none. I try not to think about that bit.

say: I'd say **families and communities** must hold each other up.
I'd want people to keep working, not just **wait for government**.
think: The buying job goes **by 2028**, even with a loyal owner.
Baking and my husband's **dairy** work are hands-on, so they last until 2031.
do: Get a **hygiene certificate** and turn the cakes into a business.
Move in with her **parents** if her pay stops.
feel: **Scared**, and a bit angry at how fast it is.
S2.quote: My father always said speed without care is how people get hurt, and the big AI companies racing each other feels like that.
fieldNote: She leans on the **hands-on** parts of her life: baking and her husband's dairy job.
Her anger goes to **big companies**, never to her loyal employer.
She sees the **double drop**: her job first, his three years later.

steps.text: Get a food hygiene certificate and set cake prices
Move in with her parents if her pay stops
Put the baby on hold until money is steadier

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people are sensible and start now. At church I'd say we should help young families plan. At work I'd ask Mr Harrow what he's thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means probably three or four more years buying. That's time to grow the cake business properly and save a bit. And maybe time to have one baby, if we're careful. It still ends, but I could build something before it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI ordering tools at work, so I'm useful for as long as possible. I'd do the hygiene certificate and get the cakes to five or six a month. And we'd save a hundred and fifty a month, and maybe try for a baby in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but hopeful too. Like I could plant something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the cake business really replace your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not all of it. A good month might bring in four hundred. But with Daniel's wage, it's the difference between managing and not. And people will always want a cake made by a person for a wedding, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Mr Harrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether he's planning to bring in the new systems, and whether he'd keep me part-time. He's always been straight with me. I'd want to plan around his answer, not guess.

I'd ask the owner **directly** what he's planning.
think: I'd get **three or four** more years of buying.

do: Learn the **AI ordering tools** at work to stay useful.
Get the **hygiene certificate** and grow to six cakes a month.
Save **a hundred and fifty** a month and try for a baby in two years.
feel: **Worried but hopeful**, like she could plant something.
S3.quote: People will always want a cake made by a person for a wedding, I hope.
fieldNote: Five years makes a **baby** possible again, which matters most to her.
The cake business is a **top-up**, not a replacement, and she knows it.
She trusts her owner to be **straight** with her.

steps.text: Learn the AI ordering tools Harrow brings in
Grow the cake business to six orders a month
Save a hundred and fifty a month towards a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so no one should panic. At church I'd say look after each other and plan sensibly. At work I'd say I'm happy to learn whatever's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm likely fine at Harrow and Sons for most of it. We could have our baby on the timeline we wanted. By the time AI could do my job, I might be ready to move into the cakes full-time anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and learn the systems when they arrive. We'd try for a baby next year, as we planned. And I'd build the cake orders slowly, so it's a real business by my mid-thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. The usual worries about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent. Every year it goes up and our pay doesn't keep up. Ten years of AI warning doesn't change the landlord's letter in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your children about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work hard and be useful to people. To learn something with their hands, like their grandmother did with her sewing. And to never be too proud to start small.

I'd say at church to **look after each other**.
think: I'm likely **fine at work** for most of the ten years.
We could have our **baby** on the timeline we wanted.
do: Keep working and learn the **systems** when they arrive.

fieldNote: The long runway returns her **family plans** to normal.

steps.text: Keep buying at Harrow and learn new systems when they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd lose both wages within three years and the baby would have to wait indefinitely. What would help is support for small family businesses like Harrow and Sons, so they can keep people on. And help for young couples starting families, not handouts, but things like cheaper childcare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the bakers. If the small bakeries close, I lose my job whatever AI does. Keeping the high street alive matters as much as any of this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: If the small bakeries close, I lose my job whatever AI does.
portrait: Yara is a 27-year-old **bakery ingredients buyer** at a loyal, family-run distributor.
She married Daniel, a **dairy night-shift worker**, last year, and they want a baby soon.
She uses AI **now and then** and would learn new tools once a colleague had them working.
In bad scenarios she delays the **baby** first and leans on her cake-baking side business.
She trusts **family and church** and blames big companies, never her employer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing both wages within three years and delaying the baby indefinitely.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small family firms** so they can keep staff.
Help for young couples, such as **cheaper childcare**.
